titre: The fire we put out too well
accroche: Since 1944, a poster bear has been teaching Americans to prevent wildfires. Putting out every fire, though, ended up creating bigger ones.
contenu_vulgarise:
Since 1944, a bear in jeans has looked out from a poster and reminded us that a forest fire, most often, starts from carelessness that could have been avoided. What the poster doesn't say is that the real problem was not only starting fewer fires. It was systematically putting out every one that started.

## A simple rule, a consequence that isn't

After the great fire of 1910, which burns more than a million hectares in Idaho and Montana in two days, the U.S. Forest Service sets itself a goal: put out every fire by ten o'clock the morning after it is reported. The rule, formalized in 1935, becomes, along with Smokey, an almost absolute policy of total suppression.

The problem is that many North American ecosystems, ponderosa pine forests, chaparral, prairies, are not simply victims of fire: they depend on it. Low-intensity, frequent fires regularly burn the brush and dead wood on the ground without touching the large trees. Systematically suppressing these small fires does not eliminate the risk: it lets fuel accumulate, year after year, until a fire, human or natural, falls on a forest that is no longer anything like a well-kept clearing.

## Yellowstone, 1988

In 1988, Yellowstone Park goes through its worst drought. Since 1972 already, the park had been letting naturally caused fires burn under monitoring, a more flexible policy than total suppression, and one that worked: between 1972 and 1987, the average fire went out on its own after burning barely one acre, about 0.4 hectare. The summer of 1988 is different: the National Park Service cites drought, high winds, and an accumulation of dry, thick fuel, without ranking these causes against one another. Nearly 321,000 hectares burn in the park, 793,880 acres, or 36% of its area. Ten thousand people and one hundred twenty million dollars in firefighting resources make no difference: it is the snow, on September 11, that finally stops the flames.

The episode is often told as proof that letting fires burn is dangerous. It shows the opposite: sixteen years of a more flexible policy had produced only minimal fires, before an exceptional drought and winds overwhelmed all the firefighting resources committed.

## A slogan that changes a word

In 1978, the Forest Service officially abandons the ten o'clock rule for a policy that allows prescribed burning. Smokey keeps his slogan until 2001, the year “forest fires” becomes “wildfires” in his campaign, a way of distinguishing accidental fires, still to be prevented, from the prescribed fires that managers now light themselves to limit the scale of the large ones.

repere.texte: In 1988, despite 10,000 people and 120 million dollars mobilized to put it out, the Yellowstone fire burns 793,880 acres, about 321,000 hectares, or 36% of the park; only the snow of September 11 ends it.
repere.source: National Park Service, “1988 Fires,” Yellowstone National Park

carte.punch: In 1988, only snow stopped the fire that 10,000 mobilized people couldn't put out.
carte.idee: Since 1935, the United States put out almost every forest fire, which lets fuel accumulate. At Yellowstone, a more flexible policy applied from 1972 produced only minimal fires, until the summer of 1988 and its 36% of the park burned despite the resources committed.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Federal wildfire policy and the legacy of suppression
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Accessible overview of a century of federal fire policy in the United States.

quiz.question: Why did the systematic suppression of all fires end up producing more destructive fires?
choix: Because the absence of small fires let pest insects proliferate much faster than before
Because drought worsened due to global warming, independently of any fire policy
Because firefighters, fewer in number after the 1978 reform, could no longer respond in time
Because it prevented regular small fires from burning off the ground fuel that had accumulated for decades
quiz.explication: Many North American ecosystems depend on frequent, low-intensity fires, which burn dead wood and brush. By systematically suppressing these small fires, the risk is not eliminated: fuel accumulates until a fire that the usual means can no longer stop.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the ten o'clock rule adopted by the U.S. Forest Service come from?
choix: It was imposed by Congress after the 1988 Yellowstone fire
It responds to the great fire of 1910, which burned more than a million hectares in two days
It was meant to limit arson fires set by farmers
It was instituted in response to the launch of the Smokey Bear campaign in 1944
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After the great fire of 1910, which burns more than a million hectares in Idaho and Montana in two days, the Forest Service sets itself the goal of putting out every fire by ten o'clock the morning after it is reported.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the natural-fire regime applied at Yellowstone between 1972 and 1987 show?
choix: That it worked: the average fire went out on its own after burning barely one acre
That it was abandoned as early as 1975, for lack of convincing results
That it was already causing fires as vast as in 1988
That it applied only to human-caused fires, never to natural ones
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Between 1972 and 1987, the park let naturally caused fires burn under monitoring: the average fire went out on its own after burning barely one acre, about 0.4 hectare, proof that the policy worked.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Forest Service change in the Smokey Bear campaign in 2001?
choix: Smokey Bear is withdrawn from all official advertising campaigns
The campaign stops targeting the general public and addresses only professionals
The slogan replaces “forest fires” with “wildfires,” to distinguish accidents from prescribed fires
The slogan calls for the first time for systematically putting out every fire
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 2001, “forest fires” becomes “wildfires” in Smokey's slogan, a way of distinguishing accidental fires, still to be prevented, from the prescribed fires that managers light themselves to limit the scale of large fires.
